fields.meta_description: Build a petition form that counts one signature per person, shows progress toward your goal and sends a signed packet to the decision-maker.
fields.h1: Build a Petition Form That Counts Every Signature Once
fields.hero_description: Describe the change you want and who decides it. Emergent builds the petition form, counts each signer once and delivers the signatures when signing closes.
fields.features_heading: What a Signature Sheet Leaves Out
fields.features_subheading: A printed sheet gives you 20 numbered rows and no way to count them. These six pieces do the counting for you.
fields.feature_1:
One signature per person

Match each new signature against the email or ID already on file. A repeat from a second device is turned away, and the signer sees a note that the first signature still counts.
fields.feature_2:
A goal counter on the signing page

Set a target before launch and show the running count on the signing page. Visitors see how close the petition is, and organizers get an email when it reaches the number promised.
fields.feature_3:
Signers your recipient will count

Ask for the detail your recipient checks, such as a lot number for an HOA board or a home address for a council. Signers outside the area go to a review list, not the total.
fields.feature_4:
Signatures drawn on screen

Let signers draw a signature with a finger or a mouse, saved with the time they signed. The printed packet puts each drawn signature beside the signer's name, as paper would.
fields.feature_5:
A packet for the person who decides

Close signing at a set date and hour. The app builds a PDF of every signature and comment, grouped by street or school, and emails it to the person who can make the change.
fields.feature_6:
Your signer list in your own codebase

Export the full code to your GitHub on paid plans once the petition outgrows one campaign. Your group hosts the signer list and reuses the form for the next issue it takes up.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Petitions and the People They Reach
fields.tab_content_1:
212 of 250 signatures, each with a street address

Alder Street has no marked crossing at the school corner, and its parents want one. They promised the Brookfield city council signatures from people who live nearby. The signing page asks every signer for a street address and shows the count as it climbs. It stands at 212 of 250, sorted by street.
fields.tab_content_2:
One student ID, one signature

Lakemont College's student senate wants the library open 24 hours during finals week. Every signer enters a student ID and a name. When ID 20418 tried to sign again from a second device, the form turned it away and kept the first signature. The senate can show the dean how each name got there.
fields.tab_content_3:
Two owners on lot 22, one signature counted

Willow Creek's bylaws let owners put an item on the board agenda once a majority of the 140 lots sign. The form asks for a lot number and counts each lot once. Both owners of lot 22 signed, and the lot shows one signature. When the count reached 71 of 140, the app emailed the board president.
fields.tab_content_4:
A signed packet on the secretary's desk before Monday

Harbor Unified's board meets on Monday, and parents want later start times at three middle schools on its agenda. Signing closed Friday at 5 p.m. The app grouped 318 signatures and 46 comments by school, built a PDF packet and emailed it to the board secretary. Each school gets its own page in the packet.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Petition Form
fields.howto_description: Start with the person who will read the petition. Every field on the form should be one they will check.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the request in one sentence
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask only for what gets checked
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide what counts as a repeat
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down who the petition is addressed to: a city council, a dean, an HOA board, or a school board. Ask how they want it delivered and whether they expect a minimum number of signatures. Their answer sets your goal.
fields.howto_step_2_des: State the change you want in one sentence a stranger understands at a glance, then add two or three short reasons. Put the request at the top of the signing page, above every field. People sign what they can read before scrolling.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for the details the recipient will use to judge a signature, such as a street address for a council or a student ID for a college. Every extra field costs you signers. Put an optional comment box last.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick the one field that identifies a signer: an email, an ID, or a lot number. A second signature with the same value gets turned away. Settle this before launch, because a total that drops later makes the whole petition look padded.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste the request, the fields, the repeat rule, and the goal into one prompt. Emergent builds the signing page and a signer table with a running count. Change any of it later by asking in a sentence, such as raising the goal to 400.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Set the close and the delivery
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose when signing closes and what the recipient receives, a PDF grouped by street or a spreadsheet. Add the recipient's email address. The packet then goes out the minute signing closes, with nobody assembling it by hand.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Sign once as a test, then sign again with the same email from your phone and confirm the repeat is turned away. Check that the counter moves and that the test packet opens. Delete the test signatures before you share the link.

plan.angle: The live top 10 splits into printable signature sheets (Venngage, WordLayouts, a council PDF, a Pinterest pin), petition platforms (Change.org, iPetitions) and two form-builder templates (Formstack, Typeform). The sheets stop at twenty numbered rows for name, address and signature; the platforms host a cause page you do not own. None of them handles what decides whether a petition lands: one signature per person, signers the recipient will count, a goal people can see, and a packet the decision-maker actually receives. This page answers the People Also Ask questions on getting, making and writing a petition, then shows four organizers whose form does that counting: a street asking a city council for a crosswalk, a student senate checking student IDs, homeowners counting one signature per lot toward a bylaw majority, and parents delivering a signed packet to a school board.
tab_stories: Parents on Alder Street ask the Brookfield city council for a crosswalk at the school corner, and their signing page shows 212 of the 250 signatures they promised the council, each tied to a street address.
The Lakemont College student senate petitions for 24-hour library access during finals, every signer enters a student ID, and a second signature from ID 20418 is turned away as a duplicate.
Willow Creek homeowners need a majority of the association's 140 lots to put repaving on the board agenda, so the form counts one signature per lot and reaches 71 lots, past the 70 required.

A parents' group at Harbor Unified closes its petition on the Friday before the school board meeting, and the app builds a packet of 318 signatures and 46 comments grouped by school and emails it to the board secretary.
